title: If three instances of a service run and another service sends a Kafka message, how do you ensure only one instance consumes it (same consumer group)?
shortTitle: Ensuring only one of three service instances consumes a Kafka message
keyPoints: Give all instances the same consumer `group.id` so Kafka divides partitions among them and each message is processed by exactly one instance.
A unique group id per instance turns each into its own group, causing every message to be processed by all instances (triple debit).
The topic needs at least as many partitions as instances for all to be active; fewer partitions means some instances sit idle.
Idempotency (unique constraint on transfer id) protects against rare duplicate delivery during rebalances with at-least-once semantics.
In Spring Boot, set `spring.kafka.consumer.group-id` once and deploy multiple instances with the same configuration.
For broadcast where every instance must see every message, give each instance a distinct group id.

s1_definition.oneliner: Give all instances the same consumer group id so each message is processed by exactly one instance.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Same group id** – configuring all service instances with an identical `group.id` so Kafka treats them as one consumer group and divides partitions among them.
- **Competing consumers** – the pattern where multiple consumers share the same group id and compete for messages, with each message going to only one consumer.
- **Broadcast pattern** – the opposite pattern where each consumer has a unique group id, so every consumer receives every message.
- **Partition count** – the maximum number of active consumers in a group; instances beyond this number sit idle as hot standbys.
- **Idempotent consumer** – a consumer that produces the same result whether it processes a message once or multiple times, protecting against rare redelivery after rebalances.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine three clerks at National Bank of India all employed on the same team to process incoming transfer slips. Because they are one team sharing one job, the supervisor hands each slip to only one clerk; the other two never see it. That is a single consumer group. If, by mistake, each clerk were treated as a separate one-person team, the supervisor would photocopy every slip and give a copy to all three, and the same transfer would be processed three times.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
Same Group ID = Single Consumption
===================================

  Producer Service
      │
      │ send("transfers", key="SAV2001", event)
      │
      ▼
  Kafka Topic: transfers (3 partitions)
  ┌──────────┬──────────┬──────────┐
  │ P0       │ P1       │ P2       │
  └────┬─────┘────┬─────┘────┬─────┘
       │          │          │
       ▼          ▼          ▼
  Group: transfer-processor
  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐
  │Instance A│ │Instance B│ │Instance C│
  │  -> P0   │ │  -> P1   │ │  -> P2   │
  └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘

  key=SAV2001 -> hash -> P2 -> Instance C ONLY

  WRONG (unique group ids):
  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐
  │Group A   │ │Group B   │ │Group C   │
  │ALL P0-P2 │ │ALL P0-P2 │ │ALL P0-P2 │
  └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘
  All 3 instances process EVERY message = triple debit!
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To ensure only one of three service instances consumes a given Kafka message, configure all three instances with the same consumer group id. Within a single consumer group, Kafka assigns each partition to exactly one consumer, so a record that lives in one partition is delivered to only one instance. In Spring Boot this is a single property: `spring.kafka.consumer.group-id=transfer-processor`, set identically on every instance.

The classic mistake is letting each instance generate a unique group id, which turns each instance into its own group and causes every message to be processed by all three instances. At National Bank of India, this would mean Rajesh gets debited three times for a single transfer. The fix is always the same: shared group id for competing consumers, unique group id only for broadcast patterns like configuration updates.

To use all three instances in parallel, the topic needs at least three partitions. With fewer partitions, some instances sit idle as hot standbys, which still provides failover. Even with the correct group id, a rebalance after a crash can cause rare redelivery, so the consumer must be idempotent: a unique constraint on the transfer id and a processed-id check ensure Rajesh is never double-debited.

Remember one sentence: same group id guarantees single consumption in the normal case, and idempotency guarantees single effect even during rare redelivery after a failover.
